name: Essays, Resumes, and Interviews
title: Essays, Resumes, and Interviews
answer: This idea sets out how AI may and may not be used when students write college essays, build resumes and practise interviews. AI can support brainstorming, organising ideas and feedback on a draft the student wrote, but it must never produce the essay or be submitted as the student's own work. It matters because an AI-written essay reveals nothing about the applicant and may break a college's own rules.

sections.body: The idea draws a line between using AI to think and using AI to produce. College essays exist so a student can show who they are, and an essay generated by AI shows nothing about the student while possibly violating a college's rules. To keep the thinking with the student, a school can offer a configured tool, such as Gemini for Education with hint only instructions, that asks questions to prompt brainstorming and reflection rather than drafting text. The same distinction applies to resumes and mock interviews, where AI can offer practice but can also let students disengage. The problem it solves is that AI makes finished-looking work easy to obtain, so schools need a clear, teachable boundary between assistance and substitution.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In high school English units, teachers have used AI to help students build resumes and to run text based practice interviews. In those units students were asked to treat the AI's output as something to examine rather than accept, and teachers built in steps requiring students to make their own choices and explain them. For college essays, the practical arrangement is a configured tool with hint only instructions that questions students to help them brainstorm and reflect, while never writing the essay itself. Students may use AI to brainstorm topics, organise ideas or get feedback on a draft they wrote, but they cannot submit AI-written text as their own. Counselors and teachers are expected to make these rules clear, and students applying to college should check each college's own stated policy on AI use in applications.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one study rather than a formal evidence label. In high school English units that used AI to help students build resumes and practise text based interviews, many students questioned and improved the AI's suggestions, but others became passive and relied on it too much (Kwon et al., 2026). Students in those units also noticed that AI responses could be generic. The finding is therefore mixed, showing both active scrutiny and passive dependence in the same setting, and it is reported for resumes and mock interviews rather than for college essays.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are stated plainly. AI must not write the essay, and students cannot submit text written by AI as their own. Colleges increasingly set their own policies on AI use in applications, and the responsibility to check those policies sits with the student, not with the tool. Teachers should build in steps that require students to make their own choices and explain them, which is the safeguard against the passivity the study observed. The judgement about what a student actually did, and what counts as their own work, stays with counselors and teachers.
